summary: Describes a framework for the operations, administration, and maintenance procedures that meet the requirements for MPLS-TP in fault, performance, and protection-switching management. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A transport network needs ways to check that its links and paths are working, to measure how well they perform, and to switch to a backup when one fails. This memo describes those checks for MPLS-TP networks. It says what each check must do without fixing the exact messages, and it requires the checks to travel the same way as the customer's data.

subtitle: The toolbox of fault, performance and lock checks that MPLS-TP transport networks use, described without tying it to one protocol.

tldr.problem: A packet transport network built on MPLS needs the same fault detection, performance measurement and protection switching that SONET/SDH and OTN networks provide, and it has to work without a control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines functional components (maintenance entities, groups, end points and intermediate points), a reference model for sections, LSPs and pseudowires, and protocol-neutral descriptions of proactive, on-demand and administrative OAM functions.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a protocol: later OAM solution documents are expected to follow the behavior it describes. It is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6435.

today: RFC 6371 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 6435. It describes a framework of behavior, not a wire protocol.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is a packet-based transport technology built on the MPLS Traffic Engineering and pseudowire (PW) data-plane architectures. It uses a set of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) procedures for fault, performance and protection-switching management that do not rely on a control plane. This framework describes those functions in a protocol-neutral way so that they meet the requirements of RFC 5860, with functionality similar to SONET/SDH and OTN OAM.

Existing MPLS OAM mechanisms are used where possible, and new ones are defined only where the existing ones are not enough. The framework applies to Sections, Label Switched Paths (LSPs), Multi-Segment Pseudowires (MS-PWs) and Sub-Path Maintenance Elements (SPMEs).

OAM packets get the same forwarding treatment as user data, which the RFC calls fate-sharing. They are told apart from data by the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) and Associated Channel Header (ACH) of RFC 5586. They are never fragmented and never share a payload with user data. The work is a joint IETF and ITU-T effort.
sections.plainLanguage: A transport network needs to check that its links and paths are working, measure how well they perform, and switch to a backup when one fails. This memo describes those checks for MPLS-TP networks. It says what each check must do, without fixing the exact messages, and it requires the checks to follow the same path as the customer's data.

sections.title: Maintenance Entities, End Points and Intermediate Points
sections.content:
OAM works on a Maintenance Entity (ME): two points on a transport path, called MEG End Points (MEPs), and the relationship between them. The MEs of one transport path that are monitored together form a Maintenance Entity Group (MEG). Between the MEPs there are zero or more MEG Intermediate Points (MIPs).

MEPs are the source and sink of OAM packets. They originate almost all proactive and on-demand OAM, and a MEP terminates all OAM packets it receives from its MEG and silently discards others. A MEP can be per-node or per-interface, and per-interface MEPs are either Up MEPs (facing the forwarding engine) or Down MEPs (facing a server layer). A MIP never sends unsolicited OAM packets; it only reacts to OAM packets from a MEP of its MEG, replying to the originating MEP. To reach a MIP, the source MEP sets the TTL to the number of hops, although the RFC warns that TTL expiry is not a fully reliable way to deliver packets because the TTL distance can change.

MEGs can be nested but not overlapped. A Sub-Path Maintenance Element (SPME) is a hierarchical LSP set up to monitor part of a path, which also provides tandem connection monitoring. A server MEP sits in the layer below and reports server-layer faults to the client layer.
sections.plainLanguage: A transport path is watched from two end points, the MEPs, which start and stop the tests. Along the way there can be intermediate points, the MIPs, which never start tests of their own but answer when a MEP asks. Groups of these points can sit inside one another, like a smaller path segment inside a longer path, but they are not allowed to overlap.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
The framework defines five kinds of MEG. Each one monitors a different thing in the stack, and each one's OAM packets fate-share with the data it monitors. They operate independently of one another, although one event such as a fiber cut can affect several at once.

The model is illustrated with a Multi-Segment Pseudowire running between two terminating provider edges across two domains. In that example, Sections, LSPs, PWs and SPMEs each have MEGs, and one node can host several MEPs. SPMEs typically monitor an OAM domain rather than the segment between two domains.

Multilink techniques such as link aggregation complicate this. If they are used, a deployment may be only partially MPLS-TP compliant, not every component link is exercised by OAM, and per-interface MIPs or Down MEPs on a multilink interface are akin to a layer violation.
sections.plainLanguage: You can watch one link between two routers, a whole path from end to end, or just a piece of a path. Each kind of watching has its own group of end points. A single failure, such as a cut cable, can affect several of these groups at the same time.

sections.title: Proactive Monitoring
sections.content:
Proactive OAM runs continuously and in service, normally between MEPs, and is set up when the transport path is created. Its functions are:

  • Continuity Check and Connectivity Verification (CC-V): the source MEP sends packets at a regular rate. A sink MEP declares a loss of continuity (LOC) defect if nothing arrives within 3.5 times its configured reception period, and a mis-connectivity defect if a packet carries an unexpected source MEP identifier. A mis-connectivity defect makes the MEP block traffic from that path; a LOC defect can block it too if the operator enabled that action.
  • Remote Defect Indication (RDI): a sink MEP tells its source MEP that a signal fail condition exists, and it can be piggy-backed on CC-V packets.
  • Alarm Reporting (AIS) and Lock Reporting (LKR): a server-layer event or locking action produces packets that let client-layer MEPs suppress secondary alarms, though they do not block traffic.
  • Packet Loss and Delay Measurement: one-way and two-way modes, using counters or timing exchanged between MEPs. One-way delay measurement needs precise time synchronization.
  • Client Failure Indication (CFI): carries a client defect to the far end when the client has no native alarm.

MIPs and intermediate nodes forward these packets as ordinary data. At start-up the source MEP function should be enabled before the sink, and at shutdown the sink should be disabled first, to avoid spurious alarms.
sections.plainLanguage: In proactive monitoring the two end points keep checking each other continuously. If the checks stop arriving for long enough, the receiving end point decides the path is broken and can stop using it. Other checks report performance figures and warn the far end that something is wrong, but they do not block traffic.

sections.title: On-Demand and Administrative Functions
sections.content:
On-demand monitoring is started by hand for a limited time, usually to find a problem. It includes on-demand connectivity verification (a MEP sends a sequence of packets to a target MEP or MIP and counts the replies), on-demand loss and delay measurement, and route tracing, which discovers the MIPs and peer MEPs along a path and, if there is a defect, traces up to it. On-demand functions need a return path.

Diagnostic tests are out of service: the MEG is locked first. Throughput estimation follows RFC 2544 by sending test packets at increasing rates and reporting the rate at which they begin to drop. Data-plane loopback sends all traffic received on the looped interface back the other way, and the only way to reach a node in that state is by TTL expiry.

The Lock Instruct (LKI) function lets one MEP instruct its peer to lock a transport path. The peer can accept or reject the instruction and replies, so the first MEP can report the real result to the network management system. If the client layer is also MPLS-TP, lock reporting starts there. Unlocking uses an LKI removal request in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Some checks are run on demand, for a short time, to find a fault. Others need the path taken out of service first, and the two ends must agree to lock it. A lock instruction is how one side asks the other side to stop using the path; the other side can agree or refuse, and says so in a reply.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OAM traffic can reveal sensitive information such as performance data and the current state of the network. Inserting or changing OAM transactions can hide the true state of the network. Administrative-control transactions such as lock or data-plane loopback instructions can be used for explicit denial-of-service attacks. For in-band messaging, the damage is limited to the entities that transit the point of malicious access, but this does not hold when an out-of-band return path is used.

The document says authentication, authorization and encryption would be one solution, but the frequency and timeliness of OAM exchanges and the many MEP-to-MEP, MEP-to-MIP and intermediate-system cases make large numbers of security associations per MEG impractical. It therefore assumes that internal links are physically secured, and that in multi-provider cases filtering or further encapsulation will constrain malicious transactions. OAM packets a node cannot recognize should be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The checks reveal a lot about how the network is doing, and fake checks could hide faults or cause trouble. Because adding strong security to every check would be too costly, the memo assumes the inside of the network is kept physically safe, and that packets a node does not recognize are thrown away.
